newsitem.title: USA: Mattel's dolls take bite out of its earnings.
newsitem.headline: Mattel's dolls take bite out of its earnings.

text.p: The doll that couldn't stop chewing took a bite out of toymaker Mattel Inc.'s fourth-quarter earnings Wednesday.

The El Segundo, Calif.-based toy giant took an $8 million charge to after-tax earnings related to its Cabbage Patch Kids Snacktime Kids dolls, pulled from the market after several children got their hair and hands stuck in the dolls' mouths.
Mattel, which offered a $40 refund to each owner of the dolls, said the move trimmed its sales by $10 million.

Mattel Chief Executive Officer Jill Barad said in a conference call with Wall Street analysts that there had been no backlash from retailers or consumers. In fact, she said, some consumers have actually been seeking the dolls as collectors' items.
"The overriding perception is that we did the right thing and we did it voluntarily," she said, adding that worldwide sales of Mattel's other Cabbage Patch dolls remained strong.

After one-time charges, Mattel's fourth-quarter profit was $113 million, or 41 cents per share, vs. $112 million, or 40 cents per share a year ago. Sales in the quarter ended Dec. 31 rose to $1.19 billion from $1.16 billion.
Investors knocked $1.25 off Mattel's stock, which ended at $27.375 on the New York Stock Exchange.

Mattel took an after-tax accounting charge of $15.1 million for royalties and other fees following a request by the Securities and Exchange Commission relating to its proposed $755 million merger with Tyco Toys Inc.
In late December, the Federal Trade Commission asked for more information regarding the proposed merger.
"We continue to have every belief that the merger will close in the first half of this year," said an attorney for Mattel.
Tyco said Tuesday it scheduled a special shareholder meeting for March 18 to vote on the merger, which analysts expect to add to Mattel's earnings by 1998.
For all of 1996, Mattel's net income was $378 million, or $1.36 per share, vs. $358 million, or $1.26 a share. Sales rose to $3.78 billion from $3.64 billion in 1995.

"Despite a difficult retail environment, worldwide sales of our four core brands of Barbie, Fisher-Price, Disney and Hot Wheels increased 10 percent in 1996, even with a 4 percent decrease in sales for Fisher-Price," Barad said in a statement accompanying the results.

Barad also told the conference call that Mattel will "pare back" its non-core brands, which have had sagging sales, and focus more on its stronger core brands. "We're now in the process of evaluating plans," she said.

"We'll see erosion in average growth (in early 1997) because we'll be managing out of some of these businesses, but we expect this year to be strong," Barad said, adding, "Our plan is to focus on core brands and maximize earnings. This new business rationale may affect our first quarter."

About 87 percent of Mattel's business is in its core brands. A Mattel spokesman said some non-core brands include games like Scrabble and UNO and Mattel's Wham-O brands, which include products like hoola hoops and Frisbee.
Tyco Toys, of Mt. Laurel, N.J., narrowed its fourth-quarter loss thanks to the unexpected popularity of the toy based on the Sesame Street character Elmo.

"The tremendous popularity of Tickle Me Elmo and the resulting broad-based sales increases in the Sesame Street product line led to 25 percent sales growth in Preschool," said Gary Baughman, chief executive officer.
For the quarter, Tyco lost $7.4 million, or 29 cents a share, on sales of $228.2 million. A year earlier it lost $17.3 million, or 52 cents a share, on sales of $215.1 million.

For the year, Tyco lost $8.8 million, or 46 cents a share, on sales of $720.9 million. It said the loss included about $7 million, or 20 cents a share, for expenses related to the pending merger with Mattel. In 1995 Tyco lost $27.2 million, or 87 cents a share, on sales of $709.1 million.
Tyco's stock ended unchanged at $11.625 on the NYSE.
